extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers and journalists (wartime public)
extracted.subtask_description: A multi-article newspaper page of Associated Press wartime coverage (political, labor, technical and human-interest items) including guidance on press behavior and descriptions of news-production technology. Targeted at general readers and news professionals following wartime developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withhold sensitive presidential travel news
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers should withhold advance publicity of the President's travels under wartime conditions until after his return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Byron Price, director of censorship, said 'the public will applaud overwhelmingly what their newspapers in withholding the news of President Roosevelt’s recent cross-country trip.' He praised press and radio cooperation and noted that advertising such travels while underway would have increased hazards; the example of Prime Minister Churchill's reported route to Russia shows the risk of broadcasting such movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid circulating information valuable to the enemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals and the public should refrain from sharing loose or self-important talk that might supply information useful to the enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Price called upon individuals 'likewise to refrain from circulating information which might prove valuable to the enemy' and stated: 'No good American, wondering why certain news does not appear in his newspaper, will fill the gap by loose and self-important talk.' This functions as a standard for civilian and press conduct during wartime reporting and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid, synchronized cablephoto/radiophoto transmission for battlefield images
rubrics_metrics.description: Battle and frontline pictures should be transmitted by cablephoto or radiophoto using synchronized sending/receiving machinery and stable short-wave or cable circuits to ensure timely, high-quality reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes the production process: pictures are placed on a sending cylinder that rotates in synchronization with a receiving cylinder in New York, scanned into electrical impulses, and converted back to light to expose film. Technical guidance and operational notes include use of short waves for steadiness (radiophoto), cable transmission methods to reduce sending time and static effects, susceptibility to sunspot/electrical disturbances causing blurred streaks, and typical transmission times cited (on the order of minutes—examples given include about 10–20 minutes after London starts sending; present transmission time noted around seven minutes in another passage). These details serve as practical standards for fast, reliable news-photo transmission.
